title: Knowledge check — 8 questions
note: Unlocks after the applied activity is submitted. Retakes are free and unlimited.

questions.prompt: Workers report AI saving roughly 11 hours a week while only 13% say their organization performs significantly better `[V]`. What best explains the gap?
options: Workers are overstating their savings to appear productive
Real relief, minus unbudgeted botsitting, minus a remainder that dissolves into the day rather than being redirected
Organizational performance measures are too crude to detect the improvement
The savings are real but take three to five years to appear in performance data
questions.explanation: No dishonesty is required. The individual experience of relief is genuine; a measured 6.4 hours goes back out as supervision nobody counts; and what's left is absorbed because almost nobody names a destination for it. A and C explain the gap by dismissing one side of it.

questions.prompt: Which of the four audit questions most often flips a workflow from positive to negative?
options: Whether final quality improved
Where the work moved to
Total human time including review and rework
What the freed capacity became
questions.explanation: Because the minutes it counts (briefing, critical reading, fixing, redoing) are precisely the minutes every vendor's arithmetic omits. D is the question that determines whether value reaches the organization, but C is the one that most often changes the sign.

questions.prompt: Your team's AI-assisted debrief process moved the work from you drafting for 40 minutes to a coordinator reviewing for 25. What does question three require you to conclude?
options: Nothing changed — the same work is being done
The workflow failed, since work should be eliminated rather than moved
The work relocated, which may well be a genuine win — but calling relocation "elimination" is how a function claims capacity it didn't create
The coordinator should be given AI tools too, to complete the elimination
questions.explanation: Relocation is often good: reviewing is usually cheaper than drafting. The error the question guards against is describing a move as a removal, which produces a capacity claim the function can't cash.

questions.prompt: The volume trap says that when content gets cheaper to produce:
options: Quality falls because less care goes into each artifact
Organizations produce more of it, moving the constraint from making work to deciding which work matters
Costs rise as consumption of AI services increases
Employees resist the new tools because output expectations rise
questions.explanation: The constraint relocates. For an HRBP that shows up as more frameworks, more decks, more survey cuts, three versions of the policy: none of which are decisions, which is the actual product. A function producing more artifacts and no more decisions has gotten worse, efficiently.

questions.prompt: IBM's widely-cited ~$300M attrition-prediction saving is best characterized as `[V]`:
options: False — the figure has been debunked
Verified, since it came from the company with access to the data
Unverifiable — a CEO claim, never independently audited or methodologically published, which disqualifies it from structural use
Irrelevant, because attrition prediction is prohibited under 101 M7
questions.explanation: Unverifiable is not the same as false, and the distinction matters: you don't have to allege dishonesty to refuse to build a business case on a number nobody can check. D overstates the line: prediction feeding *decisions about individuals* is the problem, not all attrition analysis.

questions.prompt: Why does credible proof cluster at the front door and back office rather than in assessment and prediction?
options: Vendors invest more engineering effort in transactional products
Assessment products are newer and haven't accumulated evidence yet
Transactional outcomes are countable and fail visibly, while assessment and prediction outcomes are slow and confounded — which is exactly why claims there can be loud
Regulators prohibit publishing efficacy data for assessment tools
questions.explanation: The asymmetry is about measurability, not effort or maturity. Where a failure would be obvious, claims stay modest; where attribution is nearly impossible, claims are free.

questions.prompt: What does "automating the yes is safe; automating the no is where the risk starts" mean in practice?
options: Approvals are lower-stakes decisions than rejections in every context

Accelerating someone through a process is visible and recoverable, while filtering someone out is invisible — the excluded person never appears in your data, so the failure mode is structurally unmeasurable
Rejection decisions carry more legal exposure than approval decisions
Automated approvals require less accuracy than automated rejections
questions.explanation: The heuristic is about measurability and recoverability. C is also true and is a consequence of B rather than the reason for it, and note this arrives at 101 M7's line from the evidence side rather than the ethical one.

questions.prompt: The activity asks you to name what the recovered time became, and rejects "more strategic work." Why?
options: Strategic work isn't a legitimate destination for recovered capacity
The phrase is what people say when the honest answer is "I don't know" — and an unnamed destination means the time was absorbed rather than recovered
Because only 7% of organizations provide guidance, so learners shouldn't attempt it
Because strategic work can't be measured, and the activity requires measurable outcomes
questions.explanation: The phrase functions as a placeholder for absent knowledge. A specific destination (a Module 2 quadrant, a piece of work you were skipping, hours returned to a team) is checkable in a way that "more strategic work" never is.
